---
title: "Rarefaction and other normalization methods"
format: html
editor: visual
---

The most commonly used methods to standardize sequencing depth across samples are rarefaction and data transformation. These two strategies are currently at the center of an ongoing debate in the field, as they rely on fundamentally different statistical assumptions about amplicon data. Rarefaction equalizes library sizes by subsampling reads to a common depth and has long been used in ecology, but it discards data and reduces statistical power, leading some to argue that it is statistically inadmissible [@mcmurdie2014]. Proponents of compositional data analysis emphasize that sequencing data are inherently compositional and should be analyzed using log-ratio transformations (e.g., CLR) and Aitchison geometry, rather than through subsampling (rarefaction) or count-based normalization (relative abundance) [@gloor2017]. However, rarefaction has recently been defended as a pragmatic and robust approach for controlling uneven sequencing effort in diversity analyses, emphasizing its interpretability and long-standing use in ecology [@schloss2024]. Ultimately, the debate centers on a fundamental statistical question: whether sequencing counts should be treated as compositional data requiring ratio-based transformations, or as sampling-based counts for which subsampling remains an acceptable ecological standardization strategy.

To our knowledge, rarefying can more effectively mitigate the artifact of sample library size than other normalization techniques, especially for small (\<1000 sequences per sample) and very uneven (\>\~10× on average) library sizes [@weiss2017]. Other normalization approaches are prone to generation of artifactual clusters based on sequencing depth in beta diversity analysis, and higher false discovery rates in differential abundance testing. When sequencing depth is sufficient and balanced, other compositional methods are generally better suited because they preserve statistical power [@mcmurdie2014]. For alpha diversity comparisons, rarefaction is always recommended [@schloss2024]. In any case, researchers should proceed with caution and check for library size effects if the count data was not rarefied, as demonstrated below (see [Check for library size effects](#check-for-library-size-effects)).

This section documents how to explore the sequencing depth of your samples, how to rarefy the data, how to apply other standardization methods, and how to compare them. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script `006_normalization.R` and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

```{r}

library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)
library(phyloseq)
library(dplyr)
load("../../RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

## Rarefaction

Rarefaction normalizes sequencing depth by randomly subsampling reads so that all samples have the same library size, thereby facilitating direct comparison of diversity metrics across samples. While this approach improves comparability, it inevitably discards valid observations and can lead to substantial data loss depending on the chosen rarefaction threshold.

Before rarefying, we explore how the number of OTUs depends on the number of samples and on the number of reads. Several `vegan` functions used below expect a samples x taxa matrix, so we first extract the OTU table from the `phyloseq` object.

```{r}
# Transpose the OTU table if taxa_are_rows is TRUE
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(otu_BLAST_clean), "matrix")
if (taxa_are_rows(otu_BLAST_clean)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)
```

### Species accumulation curves

Most OTUs are rare and found in only a few samples (see [Global filtering](filter/global.qmd#prevalence-of-otus)). This suggests that adding new samples to the study may lead to the continuous discovery of new OTUs. Species accumulation curves show how the total number of OTUs increases with the number of samples.

The function `vegan::specaccum()` calculates the accumulation curve of a group of samples. With `method = "random"`, samples are added in a random order, and the curve is averaged over a number of random orders (`permutations`). Here, we calculate one curve per site.

```{r}
# Identify the sites
sites <- unique(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$SiteID)

# Create an empty list to store the results of each site
accum_list <- list()

for (site in sites) {
  # Keep only the samples of the current site, and the OTUs present in them
  otu_site <- prune_samples(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$SiteID == site,
                            otu_BLAST_clean)
  otu_site <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_site) > 0, otu_site)

  # Convert to a samples x taxa matrix
  mat_site <- as(otu_table(otu_site), "matrix")
  if (taxa_are_rows(otu_site)) mat_site <- t(mat_site)

  # Run specaccum for this site
  sp <- specaccum(mat_site, method = "random", permutations = 100)

  # Save the results in a data frame
  accum_list[[site]] <- data.frame(Samples = sp$sites,
                                   Richness = sp$richness,
                                   SD = sp$sd,
                                   SiteID = site)
}

# Bind the data frames of all sites together
accum_data <- do.call(rbind, accum_list)

# Plot the accumulation curves (the ribbons show the standard deviation)
ggplot(accum_data, aes(x = Samples, y = Richness,
                       color = SiteID, fill = SiteID)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Richness - SD, ymax = Richness + SD),
              alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:max(accum_data$Samples)) +
  labs(x = "Number of samples", y = "Accumulated number of OTUs",
       title = "Species accumulation curves per site") +
  theme_classic()
```

The number of OTUs keeps increasing with the number of samples, and the curves do not reach a plateau: the fungal communities of the sites are not completely sampled. This is common in soil fungal data sets, which contain a very large number of rare OTUs.

### Rarefaction curves

To assess whether the data are suitable for rarefaction, we can draw rarefaction curves. These curves plot the expected number of observed taxa as a function of sequencing depth for each sample, allowing us to evaluate whether diversity approaches a plateau. If most curves level off near the chosen threshold, sequencing depth is likely sufficient; if they continue to rise steeply, rarefaction at that depth may lead to substantial information loss.

The function `vegan::rarecurve()` calculates the curves. With `tidy = TRUE`, it returns a data frame instead of drawing a plot, so that we can plot it with `ggplot2`. The columns are `Site` (the sample name), `Sample` (the number of reads) and `Species` (the number of OTUs). The argument `step` gives the interval (in number of reads) between the points of the curves.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
rare_curves <- rarecurve(otu_mat, step = 100, tidy = TRUE)

# Add the land use of each sample
meta_rare <- as(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean), "data.frame")
rare_curves$Land_use <- meta_rare[as.character(rare_curves$Site), "Land_use"]

# Plot the rarefaction curves, one panel per land use. The vertical line shows
# the rarefaction depth that we will choose below (1011 reads).
ggplot(rare_curves, aes(x = Sample, y = Species,
                        group = Site, color = Land_use)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1011, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ Land_use) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth (number of reads)",
       y = "Observed number of OTUs (richness)",
       color = "Land use",
       title = "Rarefaction curves") +
  theme_classic()
```

Each line is a sample. The samples have very different sequencing depths (from `r min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean))` to `r format(max(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)), big.mark = ",")` reads), and the majority of the samples are far from reaching a plateau: the more reads in a sample, the more OTUs are discovered. Let's check if this is the case.

### Sequencing depth and richness

Do samples with a higher sequencing depth also have a larger number of OTUs?

```{r}
#| output: false
# Number of OTUs per sample (richness)
seq_rich <- estimate_richness(otu_BLAST_clean, measures = "Observed")

# Add the number of reads per sample (sequencing depth)
seq_rich$reads <- sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)

min(seq_rich$Observed)  # sample with the lowest number of OTUs (36)
max(seq_rich$Observed)  # sample with the highest number of OTUs (738)
mean(seq_rich$Observed) # mean number of OTUs per sample (381)
```

```{r}
# R2 of the linear regression between number of reads and number of OTUs
r2_depth <- summary(lm(Observed ~ reads, data = seq_rich))$r.squared

ggplot(seq_rich, aes(x = reads, y = Observed)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Number of reads in the sample", y = "Number of OTUs",
       subtitle = paste("R2 =", round(r2_depth, 3))) +
  theme_bw()
```

In microbiome data, the number of reads and the number of OTUs are generally correlated: samples with more reads inevitably contain more OTUs. In this example, the number of reads explains \~50% of the variation in the number of OTUs (R^2^ = `r round(r2_depth, 2)`). Ignoring this introduces a bias in alpha diversity estimates. This is why it is important to standardize the data!

### Choose the rarefaction depth

Sequencing runs usually have uneven sequencing depths, with some samples having a low number of reads. Choosing a rarefaction depth determines which samples will be excluded from the analysis: all samples with fewer reads than the chosen depth are removed.

```{r}
# Histogram of the sequencing depths
depth_df <- data.frame(depth = sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean))

ggplot(depth_df, aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth (number of reads)", y = "Number of samples") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| output: false
# Check the number of reads of each sample, from smallest to largest
sort(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean))

# What is the smallest library size across samples? Is it sufficient?
min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)) # 120 reads

# Identify the next lowest library sizes
min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)[sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean) > 120]) # 487 reads
min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)[sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean) > 487]) # 1011 reads
```

The two samples with the smallest library sizes (120 and 487 reads) are the low-depth samples identified in [Dealing with negative controls](controls-negative.qmd). Rarefying all samples to 120 reads would discard almost all the information of the other samples. The next lowest library size is 1011 reads: if we choose this depth, we lose these two samples, but keep a reasonable number of reads in all others.

Rarefaction depth selection is inherently a trade-off between retaining samples and retaining reads per sample, and no published study provides a universally valid cutoff for the acceptable proportion of discarded samples. If several samples had a small library size, you could choose to rarefy to the size of the second, third, etc. lowest library size, until you find a sufficient depth.

### Rarefy

The function `phyloseq::rarefy_even_depth()` subsamples all samples to the same depth (`sample.size`). Samples with fewer reads are removed. Without the argument `sample.size`, the function rarefies to the library size of the sample with the lowest library size.

```{r}
#| output: false
# Choose the rarefaction depth (you can change it)
chosen_depth <- 1011

# Rarefy all samples to the chosen depth. Samples with fewer reads are removed.
otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, replace = F,
                                      sample.size = chosen_depth)

# Check the number of reads per sample: all samples should have the same depth
sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy)

# How many OTUs remained after rarefaction? OTUs that are no longer present in
# any sample are removed automatically by rarefy_even_depth().
ntaxa(otu_BLAST_clean)  # 9036 OTUs
ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy) # 5116 OTUs

# Was any sample discarded?
nsamples(otu_BLAST_clean) - nsamples(otu_table_rarefy) # 2 samples

# How many reads remain in the dataset, and what percentage of the reads is it?
sum(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy)) # 87957 reads
sum(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy)) / sum(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)) * 100 # 24.4%
```

After rarefaction, `r nsamples(otu_table_rarefy)` samples and `r ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)` OTUs remain (out of `r ntaxa(otu_BLAST_clean)`). Rarefying leads to the loss of many reads (here, \~75% of the reads), because it discards data from the samples with a high sequencing depth.

::: callout-note
Rarefaction is random: running it with a different seed gives slightly different results (e.g., a few OTUs more or less). For alpha diversity, an alternative to rarefying is to extrapolate diversity based on the accumulation of OTUs with increasing numbers of reads (see [Alpha diversity](../stats/alpha-div.qmd)). For other analyses, the [transformations](#transformations) below do not discard any reads.
:::

### Are library sizes balanced between groups?

Finally, to check whether rarefaction is needed, we can compare library sizes between groups.

```{r}
# Extract sample metadata
meta <- as(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean), "data.frame")

# Add library size
meta$library_size <- sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)

# Plot results
ggplot(meta, aes(x = SiteID, y = library_size)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw()
```

Simple statistical tests can support what we see in the boxplot.

```{r}
# Test for homogeneity of variances
bartlett.test(library_size ~ SiteID, data = meta)

# Test for differences between groups
kruskal.test(library_size ~ SiteID, data = meta)
```

These results show that the library sizes differ between sites, both in their variance (Bartlett test) and in their median (Kruskal-Wallis test): e.g., the samples of Oak_44 and Oak_54 have more reads than those of the agricultural sites. Because the number of OTUs depends on the number of reads, differences in library size between sites could be mistaken for differences in diversity. In this case, it is important to either rarefy the data, or to check that the results do not depend on library size (see [Check for library size effects](#check-for-library-size-effects)).

If the library sizes were balanced between groups (homogeneity of variance and equal medians) and sufficient in all samples (\>1000 reads per sample), other compositional methods for normalization would be better suited than rarefaction, as they do not discard any reads.

## Transformations

The advantage of other standardization methods over rarefaction is to not discard any reads. Rather than removing information, these methods transform the counts of each sample so that samples become comparable. They are more and more commonly used instead of rarefaction.

### Relative abundance transformations

#### Simple relative abundance

A simple transformation is the relative abundance: the counts of each sample are divided by the total number of reads of the sample. This method is presented here for demonstration purposes, but is not recommended in practice.

```{r}
otu_table_rel <- transform_sample_counts(
  otu_BLAST_clean, function(x) x / sum(x))
```

#### Hellinger transformation

The Hellinger transformation converts species abundances from absolute to relative values (i.e., standardizes the abundances to sample totals) and then square roots them. It is recommended to use this transformation with count data to account for the arch effect regularly observed in ecological count data, and to make Euclidean-based methods (PCA, RDA) suitable for data with many zeros [@legendre2001]. This transformation can be applied on both raw or rarefied data.

```{r}
otu_table_hel <- transform_sample_counts(
  otu_BLAST_clean, function(x) sqrt(x / sum(x)))
```

### Log-ratio transformations

Rarefaction and the Hellinger transformation preserve abundance data, which is constrained by the sample total (the compositional "closure" problem). On the other hand, ratios are invariant to total counts and therefore capture the scale-independent relationships among taxa. Log-ratio transformations thus have the advantage of solving compositionality, an important issue when doing ordinations [@gloor2017].

Because these transformations assume strictly positive data (log(0) is undefined), zero imputation is required.

::: callout-warning
Zero replacement changes the data structure and can influence downstream inference, especially when zeros are structural (the taxon is truly absent) rather than below the detection limit.
:::

#### CLR (centered log-ratio)

The CLR transformation reduces data skewness and compositionality bias. Each count is log-transformed, and the mean of the log-counts of the sample is subtracted. Here, the zeros are imputed by adding a pseudocount of 1 to all counts (x + 1). Note that the choice of pseudocount affects the result, especially for rare taxa.

```{r}
otu_table_clr <- transform_sample_counts(otu_BLAST_clean, function(x) {
  lx <- log(x + 1)
  lx - mean(lx)
})
```

#### RCLR (robust CLR)

The RCLR transformation is similar to the CLR, but only uses the non-zero values of each sample, so that it allows data that contain zeros. However, this transformation is not a per-sample operation and cannot be performed using `phyloseq::transform_sample_counts()`. We use `vegan::decostand()` instead (see `?decostand` for more information).

```{r}
# Save OTU table using a new name
otu_table_rclr <- otu_BLAST_clean

# Extract OTU table from phyloseq object and convert to a matrix
mat <- as(otu_table(otu_table_rclr), "matrix")

# If taxa are rows in OTU table, the matrix must be transposed to be used
# with vegan::decostand (remember to transpose the matrix again before
# putting it back in the phyloseq object)
taxa_rows <- taxa_are_rows(otu_table_rclr)
if (taxa_rows) mat <- t(mat) # samples = rows for vegan

# rclr transformation
mat_rclr <- decostand(mat, "rclr", impute = TRUE)

# Put back row and column names (decostand removed them)
row.names(mat_rclr) <- row.names(mat)
colnames(mat_rclr) <- colnames(mat)

# Transpose again and put it back into phyloseq object
if (taxa_rows) mat_rclr <- t(mat_rclr) # taxa = rows for phyloseq
otu_table(otu_table_rclr) <- otu_table(mat_rclr, taxa_are_rows = taxa_rows)
```

## Compare the methods

Each standardization method changes the data in a different way. To see what this means in practice, we can compare ordinations of the same samples calculated with each method. If the main patterns (e.g., the separation of the sites) are similar across methods, our conclusions do not depend on the choice of standardization. If they differ, we need to understand why before moving on to statistical analyses.

A transformation and a distance measure always go together. Some combinations are standard because the distance is suited to the values produced by the transformation:

| Standardization     | Distance                | Name of the combination   |
|---------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------|
| Rarefied counts     | Bray-Curtis             | Bray-Curtis               |
| Relative abundance  | Bray-Curtis             | Bray-Curtis               |
| Hellinger           | Euclidean               | Hellinger distance        |
| CLR                 | Euclidean               | Aitchison distance        |
| RCLR                | Euclidean               | Robust Aitchison distance |

: Table 1. Common combinations of standardization methods and distance measures

The Euclidean distance calculated on Hellinger-transformed data is called the Hellinger distance. This is the combination proposed by Legendre & Gallagher [@legendre2001], and the one implied when running a PCA or RDA on Hellinger-transformed data. The Bray-Curtis distance can also be calculated on Hellinger-transformed data, and you will find this combination in the literature, but it is less straightforward to interpret. The Bray-Curtis distance cannot be used on CLR or RCLR data, because these contain negative values.

Below, we compare four of these combinations: rarefied counts, relative abundance, Hellinger and RCLR.

### Use the same samples for all methods

The rarefied data no longer contain the two samples with a low library size, whereas the transformed data still contain them. To compare the methods, all OTU tables must contain the same samples: we remove these two samples from the transformed data too.

```{r}
keep_samples <- sample_names(otu_table_rarefy)

otu_table_rel  <- prune_samples(keep_samples, otu_table_rel)
otu_table_hel  <- prune_samples(keep_samples, otu_table_hel)
otu_table_rclr <- prune_samples(keep_samples, otu_table_rclr)
```

The transformations are calculated for each sample separately, so removing samples afterwards does not change the values of the other samples. The only exception is the zero imputation of the RCLR transformation, which uses the whole table; the effect of the two removed samples is negligible.

### Calculate the distance matrices

The function `phyloseq::distance()` calculates a distance matrix between samples from a `phyloseq` object. It uses `vegan::vegdist()` for most distance measures. We will use the distance matrices to compare the methods directly (see [Compare the distance matrices](#compare-the-distance-matrices)).

```{r}
# 1. Rarefied counts + Bray-Curtis
dist_rare <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rarefy, method = "bray")

# 2. Relative abundance + Bray-Curtis
dist_rel <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rel, method = "bray")

# 3. Hellinger + Euclidean (= Hellinger distance)
dist_hel <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_hel, method = "euclidean")

# 4. RCLR + Euclidean (= robust Aitchison distance)
dist_rclr <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rclr, method = "euclidean")
```

::: callout-note
`vegan::vegdist()` can also calculate the Aitchison and robust Aitchison distances directly from the raw counts, without transforming the data first, e.g., `vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison")`. This gives a different result from the code above, because the zeros are handled differently: we imputed them with `decostand()` when creating `otu_table_rclr` (`impute = TRUE`), whereas `vegdist()` does not impute them. Be consistent and report which approach you used.
:::

### NMDS ordinations

NMDS (non-metric multidimensional scaling) represents the distances between samples in a small number of dimensions (here, `k = 2`). NMDS only uses the rank order of the distances, which makes it suitable for any distance measure.

The function `phyloseq::ordinate()` calculates the distance matrix and runs the NMDS (`vegan::metaMDS()`) in one step. The distance measure is given by its name, e.g., `distance = "bray"`. Additional arguments are passed on to `metaMDS()`:

-   `k`: number of dimensions of the ordination;
-   `trymax`: maximum number of random starts used to find the best solution. NMDS is an iterative method that starts from random configurations. The seed set at the start of the script makes the results reproducible, as long as the script is run from the start;
-   `autotransform = FALSE`: by default, `metaMDS()` applies a square root and a Wisconsin double standardization to count data. We turn this off, so that each ordination is calculated on the data as we transformed them above;
-   `trace = FALSE`: hides the progress messages.

::: callout-warning
`ordinate()` also accepts a distance matrix that was already calculated (e.g., `distance = dist_rare`), but in that case it ignores all additional arguments and silently uses the default settings of `metaMDS()`.
:::

```{r}
nmds_rare <- ordinate(otu_table_rarefy, method = "NMDS", distance = "bray",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)
nmds_rel  <- ordinate(otu_table_rel, method = "NMDS", distance = "bray",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)
nmds_hel  <- ordinate(otu_table_hel, method = "NMDS", distance = "euclidean",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)
nmds_rclr <- ordinate(otu_table_rclr, method = "NMDS", distance = "euclidean",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)
```

Printing an NMDS object shows the stress and whether a convergent solution was found. If it says "Best solution was not repeated", increase `trymax` before interpreting the ordination.

```{r}
nmds_rare
```

The stress value indicates how well the 2D ordination represents the original distances. As a rule of thumb, stress \< 0.1 is good, 0.1-0.2 is acceptable, and \> 0.2 should be interpreted with caution.

```{r}
nmds_stress <- c(Rarefied  = nmds_rare$stress,
                 RelAbund  = nmds_rel$stress,
                 Hellinger = nmds_hel$stress,
                 RCLR      = nmds_rclr$stress)
round(nmds_stress, 3)
```

To compare the ordinations, we plot them side by side, with the samples coloured by site. The stress value is added to each plot.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 9
plot_nmds <- function(physeq, ord, title) {
  plot_ordination(physeq, ord, color = "SiteID") +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = paste("Stress =", round(ord$stress, 3))) +
    theme_bw()
}

p_rare <- plot_nmds(otu_table_rarefy, nmds_rare, "Rarefied + Bray-Curtis")
p_rel  <- plot_nmds(otu_table_rel,    nmds_rel,  "Relative abundance + Bray-Curtis")
p_hel  <- plot_nmds(otu_table_hel,    nmds_hel,  "Hellinger + Euclidean")
p_rclr <- plot_nmds(otu_table_rclr,   nmds_rclr, "RCLR + Euclidean (robust Aitchison)")

ggarrange(p_rare, p_rel, p_hel, p_rclr,
          ncol = 2, nrow = 2, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "right")
```

When comparing the plots, keep in mind that the orientation of NMDS axes is arbitrary: an ordination can be rotated or mirrored without changing its meaning. Focus on which samples group together and which groups are separated, not on the position of the groups in the plot.

### Compare the distance matrices

The plots give a visual impression, but we can also measure how similar the methods are. The Mantel test calculates the correlation between two distance matrices. A correlation close to 1 means that both methods rank the distances between samples in the same way.

```{r}
dist_list <- list(Rarefied  = dist_rare,
                  RelAbund  = dist_rel,
                  Hellinger = dist_hel,
                  RCLR      = dist_rclr)

# Create an empty matrix to store the Mantel correlations
mantel_r <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(dist_list), ncol = length(dist_list),
                   dimnames = list(names(dist_list), names(dist_list)))

# Calculate the Mantel correlation (Spearman) for each pair of methods
for (i in names(dist_list)) {
  for (j in names(dist_list)) {
    mantel_r[i, j] <- mantel(dist_list[[i]], dist_list[[j]],
                             method = "spearman", permutations = 0)$statistic
  }
}
round(mantel_r, 2)
```

Here, `permutations = 0` skips the permutation test, because we are only interested in the correlation. Distances between the same samples are not independent, so we would not interpret a p-value in this context.

Rarefaction and relative abundance usually give very similar results, as both are based on proportions. The RCLR transformation is usually the most different, because it gives more weight to rare taxa, whereas Bray-Curtis is dominated by the most abundant taxa.

In this example, the rarefied, relative abundance and Hellinger distances are almost identical (r ≥ 0.97), and the four NMDS plots show a similar overall pattern: the agricultural sites and the grassland separate from the oak forests. The RCLR distances are less correlated with the others (r \~ 0.6): with RCLR, the grassland separates more strongly from the agricultural sites, whereas the old oak forest (Oak_ref) is less distinct from the other oak forests. Note also the much lower stress of the RCLR ordination.

### Check for library size effects

If the data are not rarefied, differences in library size between samples can still affect the results. A simple way to check for this is to test whether library size explains a part of the variation in the ordinations.

The function `vegan::envfit()` fits a variable onto an ordination and tests how much of the variation in sample positions it explains (r^2^). We use the original library sizes (before rarefaction) for all methods, so that we can check whether each method has removed the effect of sequencing depth. Library sizes are log-transformed because they vary over an order of magnitude.

```{r}
# Original library sizes of the samples used in the ordinations, in the same
# sample order as the ordinations
log_lib <- data.frame(
  log_library_size = log10(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)[keep_samples]))

ord_list <- list(Rarefied  = nmds_rare,
                 RelAbund  = nmds_rel,
                 Hellinger = nmds_hel,
                 RCLR      = nmds_rclr)

# Fit library size onto each ordination and store the r2 and p-values
lib_fit <- t(sapply(ord_list, function(ord) {
  fit <- envfit(ord, log_lib, permutations = 999)
  c(r2 = unname(fit$vectors$r), p = unname(fit$vectors$pvals))
}))
round(lib_fit, 3)
```

A low r^2^ and a non-significant p-value mean that library size does not explain the position of the samples in the ordination. If library size has a strong effect with the transformations, but not with rarefaction, consider using rarefied data. Note that if library size differs between groups (which we tested [above](#are-library-sizes-balanced-between-groups)), its effect cannot be separated from the effect of the groups.

In this example, library size has no significant effect on the rarefied ordination (p \> 0.05), but it explains a small and significant part of the variation in the relative abundance, Hellinger and RCLR ordinations (p \< 0.05). A likely reason is that deeper sequenced samples detect more rare taxa (fewer zeros), which affects the transformations that do not discard reads. However, we saw above that library sizes also differ between sites: part of this effect may be due to the sites themselves.

For a visual check, the ordinations can also be coloured by library size:

```{r}
sample_data(otu_table_rclr)$log_library_size <- log_lib$log_library_size

plot_ordination(otu_table_rclr, nmds_rclr, color = "log_library_size") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "RCLR + Euclidean, coloured by library size") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Which method to choose?

This demonstration shows why it is important to check for library size effects when the data are not rarefied. With the low and uneven sequencing depth of this ITS data set, and library sizes that differ between sites, rarefied data are a safe choice. In this workflow:

-   [Alpha diversity](../stats/alpha-div.qmd) is compared on data rarefied to 1011 reads, and with rarefaction/extrapolation curves (`iNEXT`), which use all reads;
-   [Beta diversity](../stats/beta-div.qmd) and the following analyses compare several transformations (e.g., Hellinger on rarefied data, and CLR for the Aitchison distance).

Each of these scripts starts again from `otu_BLAST_clean.RData` and applies the standardization it needs, using the code shown on this page.

::: callout-important
Whichever method you choose, report it (including the rarefaction depth or the pseudocount), and check that your conclusions do not depend on it.
:::
